description: When a Georgia teenager is hurt in a wreck over holiday break, several insurance policies may apply. Here is whose coverage pays, and what to do.
shortAnswer: The answer is almost never just one policy. It depends on who was driving, whose car it was, and who caused the wreck. Your own uninsured motorist coverage often protects your teenager even when riding in someone else’s car.

sections.heading: First, the rules your teenager is driving under
sections.shortAnswer: Under O.C.G.A. § 40-5-24, a Class D driver cannot drive between midnight and 5 a.m. and is limited in how many non-family passengers under 21 can ride along. Breaking those rules can be evidence of negligence, but it does not decide a case alone.

sections.heading: If your teen was a passenger in a friend’s car
sections.shortAnswer: The car’s liability coverage, the driver’s own coverage, the friend’s parents under the family purpose doctrine, and your own uninsured motorist coverage may all apply.

sections.heading: If your teen was driving and someone else caused it
sections.shortAnswer: The at-fault driver’s liability coverage pays first, and your own UM coverage is there for the amount it does not cover. Your MedPay can help with medical bills while you wait.

sections.heading: If your teen was driving and caused the wreck
sections.shortAnswer: Friends hurt in your car look to your liability coverage. Household exclusions limit coverage for brothers and sisters, but Georgia courts have generally enforced them only above the minimum limits.

sections.heading: Children who are home from college
sections.shortAnswer: An 18-year-old is a legal adult, so the claim belongs to the student. Whether the student still counts as a resident relative under your policy depends on the policy wording and the student’s intent to come home.

sections.heading: Parties and alcohol
sections.shortAnswer: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-1-40(b), a person who knowingly furnishes alcohol to someone under 21, knowing that person will soon be driving, can be liable for the harm the drunk driver causes.

sections.heading: Phones
sections.shortAnswer: Georgia’s hands-free law bars drivers from holding a phone while driving. Phone records are often the most important evidence in a teen driver case, and a lawyer can send a preservation letter right away.

sections.heading: Seat belts
sections.shortAnswer: After Georgia’s 2025 tort reform, a jury can now hear whether an injured person was wearing a seat belt.

sections.heading: What I tell parents before break
sections.shortAnswer: Know your liability and UM limits, make sure every licensed teenager is on the policy, consider an umbrella policy, and talk with your teenager about the passenger limits, the curfew and seat belts.

sections.heading: What I tell parents after a wreck
sections.shortAnswer: Get medical care, get the other driver’s insurance at the scene, report the wreck to your own insurer, do not give recorded statements, and do not sign a release before a lawyer reads it.

faq.q: Does my auto insurance cover my teenager if they are hurt riding in a friend’s car in Georgia?
faq.a: Often, yes. Your teenager is probably an insured under your own auto policy’s uninsured motorist coverage, even riding in someone else’s car. Since 2009, Georgia UM coverage is ordinarily added on top of the at-fault driver’s liability coverage unless you chose the reduced type in writing.

faq.q: What are Georgia’s passenger limits for a 16- or 17-year-old driver?
faq.a: Under O.C.G.A. § 40-5-24, a Class D driver cannot carry any non-family passenger during the first six months, no more than one non-family passenger under 21 during the second six months, and no more than three non-family passengers under 21 after that. A Class D driver also cannot drive between midnight and 5 a.m.

faq.q: Can someone who gave alcohol to a teenager be liable for a drunk-driving wreck in Georgia?
faq.a: Yes, in some cases. Under O.C.G.A. § 51-1-40(b), a person who knowingly furnishes alcohol to someone under 21, knowing that person will soon be driving, can be liable for the harm the drunk driver causes. Simply owning the house where teenagers drank is not enough.
